topics.title: Front matter
topics.plain_summary: This part of the document is front matter (cover, contents, or lists) rather than policy itself.

topics.title: 2026 Budget Presentation and Statutory Reports
topics.plain_summary: The government presented the 2026 Budget Statement and Economic Policy, along with required annual reports on petroleum funds and the African Union Import Levy, for parliamentary approval.
topics.why_it_matters: This budget sets the financial and economic rules for the entire country for the year, dictating how public funds are managed and which sectors receive government attention.
key_changes: The Budget Statement and Economic Policy of Government for the year ending 31st December 2026 was moved for parliamentary approval.

topics.title: New Bills, Regulations, and Policy Requests for 2026
topics.plain_summary: The government is introducing several new bills, regulations, and policy updates, including repealing the COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy, amending VAT, GETFund, and National Health Insurance laws, and implementing an AI-powered trade data analytics system for customs.
topics.why_it_matters: These legal changes affect taxes, healthcare funding, education resources, and trade regulations, directly altering the financial obligations and benefits experienced by citizens and business owners.
key_changes: The Value for Money Bill; The Virtual Asset Service Providers Bill; The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Bill; The COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy (Repeal) Bill; The Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund) (Amendment) Bill; The National Health Insurance (Amendment) Bill; The Public Procurement Regulations

topics.title: 2026 National Minimum Wage and Economic Dialogue
topics.plain_summary: Government, organized labor, and employers agreed on the National Minimum Wage and Base Pay for 2026, establishing the National Tripartite Committee as a permanent forum for ongoing economic dialogue.
topics.why_it_matters: Workers will receive agreed-upon minimum wages and base pay for 2026, while a permanent forum will give labor and employers continuous input into economic and job-creation policies.
key_changes: Together with Government, we have successfully agreed on the National Minimum Wage and Base Pay for 2026, ahead of this Budget...

topics.title: Strategic Priorities for Growth, Jobs, and Transformation
topics.plain_summary: The government outlined three main strategic priorities for 2026: consolidating macroeconomic stability, accelerating economic transformation and job creation through initiatives like the 24-Hour Economy and Big Push Infrastructure Agenda, and strengthening security and social sectors.
topics.why_it_matters: These priorities aim to create sustainable jobs, improve public infrastructure, modernize education and healthcare, and extend essential utilities like electricity and water to communities across all 16 regions.
key_changes: Consolidating Macroeconomic Stability
Accelerating Economic Transformation and Job Creation
Strengthening Security and Social Sectors for Inclusive Growth

topics.title: Global Economic Developments and Inflation Outlook
topics.plain_summary: Global economic growth is expected to stay modest at 3.2 percent in 2025 and 3.1 percent in 2026. Across the world, inflation is gradually slowing down due to better supply chains and tighter monetary policies. In Sub-Saharan Africa, average inflation is projected to drop from 13.1 percent in 2025 to 10.9 percent in 2026, though everyday people may still face challenges from food price changes and climate shocks.
topics.why_it_matters: When global inflation and commodity prices change, it directly affects the cost of imported goods, food prices, and the cost of living for ordinary citizens. A drop in regional inflation means price increases could start slowing down, giving households some relief on everyday expenses.
key_changes: Global growth is projected at 3.2 percent in 2025 and 3.1 percent in 2026.
Sub-Saharan Africa’s growth is projected at 4.1 percent in 2025 and 4.4 percent in 2026.

topics.title: Commodity Market Trends and Prices
topics.plain_summary: Global commodity prices are seeing mixed trends. Crude oil and gold prices are shifting, while cocoa prices spiked due to poor weather and lower production in West Africa, though prices are expected to stabilize as supply improves.
topics.why_it_matters: Changes in global commodity prices directly impact farmers who grow cash crops like cocoa, as well as businesses and consumers who rely on fuel and imported goods tied to global oil prices.
key_changes: Brent crude oil prices are expected to average US$68 per barrel in 2025, down from US$79 in 2024.
Cocoa prices have surged to an average of US$7,800 per metric tonne in 2025, up from US$5,900 in 2024, due to adverse weather and production shortfalls in West Africa.

topics.title: Ghana’s Progress Toward ECOWAS Macroeconomic Convergence
topics.plain_summary: Ghana has met five out of the six ECOWAS convergence criteria by the third quarter of 2025, including maintaining zero central bank financing of the budget, keeping debt below the 70 percent benchmark, and holding external reserves that cover 4.8 months of imports.
topics.why_it_matters: Meeting regional convergence criteria reflects strong national financial health, which helps stabilize exchange rates, control inflation, and attract investment.
key_changes: In 2025, the fiscal deficit is projected at 2.8 percent of GDP, below the 3 percent benchmark.
Gross external reserves now cover 4.8 months of imports, exceeding the minimum threshold of three months.
By the third quarter of 2025, Ghana had met five out of the six ECOWAS convergence criteria.

sections.title: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025
sections.heading: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Macroeconomic Targets and Economic Recovery
topics.plain_summary: Ghana's economy has turned a corner in 2025, with overall GDP expanding by 6.3 percent in the first half of the year, beating the annual projection of 4.8 percent. Inflation dropped from 23.8 percent in December 2024 to 8 percent in October 2025, bringing single-digit inflation back for the first time in four years. The Bank of Ghana cut the monetary policy rate from 28 percent to 21.5 percent.
topics.why_it_matters: The dramatic drop in inflation and the lowering of the policy rate bring real relief to households and businesses by lowering the cost of credit, stabilizing prices, and easing the financial pressures experienced in previous years.
key_changes: Overall real GDP expanded by 6.3 percent in the first half of 2025.
Inflation declined sharply to 8 percent in October 2025.
The monetary policy rate was reduced by 650 basis points to 21.5 percent.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Real Sector Performance across Services and Agriculture
topics.plain_summary: Growth in the real sector was broad-based, led by the services and agriculture sectors. The services sector grew by 8.8 percent, boosted by IT and communication, financial and insurance, and the education sub-sectors. Agriculture grew by 6.0 percent, with cocoa production recovering to a positive 2.8 percent growth.
topics.why_it_matters: Stronger performance in agriculture and services directly improves farm incomes, boosts educational enrollment and support programs, and drives job creation across the country.
key_changes: Services sector grew by 8.8 percent in the first half of 2025.
Agriculture sector grew by 6.0 percent in the first half of 2025.
Cocoa production rebounded to a positive 2.8 percent growth.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Fiscal Performance, Arrears Audit, and Public Debt Reduction
topics.plain_summary: The government achieved a primary surplus of 1.6 percent of GDP by September 2025. A special audit of inherited payables worth GH¢68.8 billion rejected GH¢10.4 billion in fraudulent or unsupported claims, saving the public purse. Public debt dropped from 61.8 percent of GDP at the end of 2024 to 45.0 percent by October 2025, and treasury bill rates fell significantly.
topics.why_it_matters: Cutting unverified public arrears protects taxpayer money from waste. Lower domestic borrowing costs make it easier for the government to finance operations without squeezing out private sector credit.
key_changes: Primary balance on a commitment basis recorded a surplus of 1.6 percent of GDP.
Public debt to GDP ratio reduced to 45.0 percent by October 2025.
The 91-day Treasury-bill rate declined to around 10.6 percent by October 2025.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Energy Sector Reforms and Power Purchase Agreements
topics.plain_summary: The government successfully renegotiated Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with Independent Power Producers (IPPs), saving over $250 million and reprofiling $1.1 billion in legacy debt. Tariffs for solar projects were reduced from 18 cents to 6.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, and the Cash Waterfall Mechanism raised ECG monthly revenues.
topics.why_it_matters: Fixing the energy sector debt and lowering renewable tariffs makes electricity generation more financially sustainable and helps prevent future power crises or sudden tariff hikes for consumers.
key_changes: Renegotiated all PPAs with IPPs, saving over $250 million.
Reduced solar project tariffs from 18 cents to 6.5 cents per kilowatt-hour.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Cocoa Sector Turnaround and Pricing
topics.plain_summary: The COCOBOD Turnaround Strategy set the producer price of cocoa at GH¢58,000 per tonne for the 2025/26 crop season, representing about 68 percent of the international FOB price. Cocoa roads contracts were rationalized from GH¢21 billion to GH¢6 billion.
topics.why_it_matters: Higher farm-gate prices directly improve the livelihoods of cocoa farmers and reduce the incentive for smuggling, while streamlining cocoa road debts frees up funds for core agricultural productivity.
key_changes: Producer price of cocoa set at GH¢58,000 per tonne for the 2025/26 season.
Cocoa roads contracts rationalized from GH¢21 billion to GH¢6 billion.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Import Declaration Forms (IDF) Abuse and Enforcement
topics.plain_summary: An assessment of import processes revealed massive abuse of Import Declaration Forms (IDFs), with an equivalent of $31 billion transferred abroad between April 2020 and August 2025 with no corresponding goods imported. Cases have been referred to law enforcement, and new audits are put in place.
topics.why_it_matters: Cracking down on fraudulent foreign exchange transfers and tax evasion through fake imports helps protect foreign exchange reserves, stabilizes the Cedi, and retains funds for national development.
key_changes: An Inter-Agency Committee will audit all import-related transfers going forward.
The Bank of Ghana will match every foreign exchange transfer with verified import data.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: External Sector and Exchange Rate Strengthening
topics.plain_summary: The Ghana Cedi strengthened significantly against major international currencies, appreciating by 34.6 percent against the US Dollar, 28.0 percent against the British Pound, and 20.5 percent against the Euro by November 2025. Gross international reserves rose to about $11.4 billion (4.8 months of import cover).
topics.why_it_matters: A stronger Cedi and higher foreign reserves lower the cost of imported goods, reduce the domestic cost of servicing external debt, and help stabilize consumer prices.
key_changes: The Cedi appreciated by 34.6 percent against the US Dollar by November 2025.
Gross international reserves increased to approximately $11.4 billion.

source_references.section: SECTION 3: STATE OF GHANA’S ECONOMY IN 2025

topics.title: Governance and Public Administration Reforms
topics.plain_summary: The government is updating decentralisation laws, expanding passport services with chip-embedded biometric documents, and implementing the Human Resource Management Information System to clean up public payrolls and streamline civil service operations.
topics.why_it_matters: These changes impact how citizens interact with public offices, apply for travel documents, and access local government services. Civil servants experience more centralized and digitized human resource management, while small business owners and entrepreneurs benefit from improved microfinance support and streamlined business registration processes, leading to greater efficiency and less red tape in public service delivery.
key_changes: The Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Decentralisation initiated the development of a Five-Year National Decentralisation Policy (2026–2030), due for finalisation by November 2025. Concurrently, the Legislative Review Committee began reviewing critical laws , including the Local Governance Act, 2016 (Act 923) and the Pre-tertiary Education Act, 2020 (Act 1049), to harmonise our decentralisation framework. These amended laws will be submitted to Parliament in 2026.

topics.title: Economic Policy, Tax, and Financial Sector Reforms
topics.plain_summary: The Ministry of Finance is strengthening fiscal discipline through enhanced procurement rules, expanding climate finance and sovereign insurance for farmers, and reviewing tax laws to improve fairness while working under IMF-supported economic recovery programs.
topics.why_it_matters: The average person and local businesses benefit from macroeconomic stability, lower inflation pressures, and targeted safety nets such as drought and flood insurance for vulnerable areas. Taxpayers and traders experience clearer dispute resolution mechanisms and reviewed tax codes, while public procurement rules protect state resources from unauthorized spending.
key_changes: The enactment of the Public Procurement (Amendment) Act, 2025 (Act 1139) introduced mandatory commitment authorisation, verification of public payments, and strict penalties for unauthorised commitments, marking a decisive step toward restoring fiscal discipline and preventing arrears accumulation.

topics.title: Agriculture, Fisheries, and Natural Resource Management
topics.plain_summary: The government is scaling up agricultural inputs, irrigation projects, and seed distribution under the Feed Ghana Programme while cracking down on illegal mining and promoting responsible cooperatives and gold traceability.
topics.why_it_matters: Farmers gain better access to subsidized seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation facilities, which helps reduce food prices and secure year-round yields. Small-scale miners and fishing communities operate under formalized cooperatives and new environmental protections, safeguarding water bodies and marine resources for long-term community livelihoods.
key_changes: Beginning in 2026, it will roll out a comprehensive Gold Traceability System, ensuring every gram of gold purchased can be traced to its verified, licensed, and environmentally compliant origin.

topics.title: Infrastructure and Transport Development
topics.plain_summary: Major investments are underway in road corridors, railway lines, affordable housing units, and digital connectivity to improve transportation safety, reduce urban congestion, and connect production zones to ports.
topics.why_it_matters: Citizens enjoy faster travel times, reduced freight costs, and improved road safety through ongoing highway construction and expanded public mass transit fleets. Low- and middle-income earners gain access to affordable housing options and expanded rent-to-own schemes, while rural communities benefit from extended digital telecommunication coverage.
key_changes: The Saglemi Affordable Housing Project is being redesigned for completion through a public-private partnership model. A total of 8,000 units are expected to be made habitable under the first phase in 2026.

topics.title: Social Sector, Education, and Healthcare Expansion
topics.plain_summary: The government is reforming basic and senior high school curricula, expanding tertiary education access with new universities, increasing health facility reconstruction, and reinforcing social protection grants for vulnerable groups.
topics.why_it_matters: Students benefit from modernized curricula, expanded technical and vocational training, and fee policies in higher education. Patients experience improved healthcare access through upgraded regional hospitals and community health compounds, while teachers and healthcare professionals receive better housing support and prompt payment of allowances.
key_changes: In 2026, Government will overhaul the basic school curriculum from kindergarten to primary six to equip learners with practical skills in moral integrity, electronics, robotics, coding, and artificial intelligence, preparing them for the modern economy.

topics.title: Public Safety, Justice, and Anti-Corruption
topics.plain_summary: Law enforcement agencies are strengthening border security, digitizing court records, recovering misappropriated public funds through payroll audits, and expanding free legal aid services to vulnerable citizens.
topics.why_it_matters: Citizens and vulnerable persons gain enhanced protection of their human rights, greater access to free legal representation, and faster justice delivery through digitized court systems and alternative dispute resolution. The public benefits from stricter anti-corruption measures, payroll cleaning that saves state funds, and more responsive security services.
key_changes: In 2026, the Legal Aid Commission will open new regional offices in Oti and Bono East, and district offices in Adentan, Jirapa, and Busunya to expand access to justice nationwide.

sections.title: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS
sections.heading: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Macroeconomic Policy Objectives and Targets
topics.plain_summary: The government is setting clear economic goals for 2026 and the medium term to keep inflation low, support growth, and maintain fiscal discipline. This means aiming for a real GDP growth of at least 4.8 percent in 2026 and keeping inflation around 8.0 percent by the end of the year. For the average person, these targets aim to lower the cost of living, stabilize prices, and create jobs.
topics.why_it_matters: Keeping inflation at 8 percent and growing the economy by nearly 5 percent helps reduce the daily cost of living for families and households. A stable economy protects people's savings and creates an environment where businesses can hire more workers and offer decent jobs.
key_changes: Overall real GDP growth of at least 4.8 percent, driven by continued expansion in services, manufacturing, and agriculture
Non-oil real GDP growth of at least 4.9 percent
End-year inflation of 8.0 percent
A primary surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP on commitment basis
Gross international reserves of not less than three months of import cover

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Fiscal Policy and Revenue Mobilisation
topics.plain_summary: The government is planning its budget for 2026 with total expenditures programmed at GH¢302.5 billion, balancing spending on infrastructure and public services with strict financial discipline. Public workers will see a 9 percent negotiated increase in base pay under the Single Spine Salary Structure. To fund development without overburdening current taxpayers, the government plans to use digital tax systems and broaden the tax base.
topics.why_it_matters: Public sector workers benefit directly from the 9 percent pay raise. At the same time, targeted government spending on roads, education, and health aims to improve public infrastructure and deliver better basic services to communities across the country.
key_changes: Total Expenditure on commitment basis for 2026 has been programmed at GH¢302.5 billion, representing 18.9 percent of GDP
Compensation of Employees projected at GH¢90.8 billion, reflecting the 9% negotiated increase in base pay for public servants under the Single Spine Salary Structure
Total Revenue and Grants projected at GH¢268.1 billion, up from GH¢226.5 billion in 2025

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Drivers of Growth, Jobs, and Business Reforms
topics.plain_summary: To foster job creation and economic transformation, the government is rolling out policies to make starting and growing a business easier. This includes 24/7 business registration centers, digital helplines, and support for agriculture and agribusiness. Programs like the National Apprenticeship Programme, the 24-Hour Economy, and the Big Push infrastructure project are designed to build roads, connect farming communities, and expand vocational training.
topics.why_it_matters: Entrepreneurs and small business owners will face fewer bureaucratic hurdles when registering and operating businesses. Young people and job seekers will benefit from expanded vocational training, agricultural programs, and improved infrastructure that opens up markets and generates local employment.
key_changes: Establishing 24/7 business registration centres and digital helplines, and submitting new Consumer Protection, Competition, and Business Regulatory Reform Bills to Parliament
Rolling out a five-year Trade Sector Support Programme and helping firms leverage AfCFTA
Expanding access to vocational training through the National Apprenticeship Programme

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

topics.title: Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy
topics.plain_summary: The government is implementing a debt management strategy for 2025–2028 to keep public borrowing sustainable and transparent. Following major debt restructuring, the strategy aims to lower refinancing and interest rate risks, resume benchmark bond issuances in 2026 to support market liquidity, and rely primarily on concessional loans from international partners.
topics.why_it_matters: Prudent management of public debt reduces the amount of national revenue spent on paying off interest. This frees up crucial funds that the government can redirect toward public infrastructure, schools, hospitals, and social programs that directly benefit citizens.
key_changes: Debt maturing within one year will not exceed 15±5 percent of total debt
Average time to maturity will remain at eight years or more
The share of Treasury bills will be capped at 20±5 percent of domestic debt
USD-denominated debt will not exceed 70 percent of external debt

source_references.section: SECTION 5: 2026 MEDIUM-TERM POLICY OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS

sections.title: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES
sections.heading: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Value Added Tax (VAT) Reforms
topics.plain_summary: The government is introducing major reforms to the Value Added Tax (VAT) system to make it simpler, fairer, and less burdensome for both households and businesses. These changes include abolishing specific levies, reducing the effective rate, and raising the registration threshold so that smaller businesses are not forced to charge VAT.
topics.why_it_matters: These VAT changes directly put money back into the pockets of everyday citizens and businesses by lowering costs and removing cumbersome administrative hurdles for small traders. By raising the registration threshold and removing extra levies, running a small business becomes easier and everyday items can become more affordable.
key_changes: Abolish the COVID-19 Health Recovery Levy
Abolish the decoupling of the GETFund and NHIL levies from the VAT tax base, allowing both levies to be subject to input tax deductions
Abolish VAT on reconnaissance and prospecting of minerals
Reduce the effective VAT rate from 21.9% to 20%
Raise the VAT registration threshold from GH¢200,000 to GH¢750,000
Extend the VAT zero-rating on the supply of locally manufactured textiles to 2028

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Establishment of the Value for Money Office (VfMO)
topics.plain_summary: The government is setting up a new independent office to oversee public spending before contracts are awarded. This watchdog will check project costs, ensure fair pricing, and cut down on waste and inflated contract prices.
topics.why_it_matters: This office acts as a permanent guardian of public funds to stop corruption and inflated pricing on public projects. For the average person, it means public money saved on waste can instead be redirected to build better roads, schools, and hospitals.
key_changes: Establish an independent statutory VfMO with legal power to review, certify, and sanction.
Implement pre-award reviews to certify scope, cost, financing, and timelines before approval.
Implement post-award monitoring to prevent overruns and enforce quality during delivery.
Implement post-completion evaluations to confirm value created.

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Rural Electricity Acceleration and Urban Intensification Initiative
topics.plain_summary: To achieve universal electricity access, the government is launching an initiative starting in 2026 to connect unserved and underserved communities, homes, schools, and businesses to the national grid.
topics.why_it_matters: Access to reliable electricity is vital for daily living, education, and local economic activity. This initiative ensures that families living in remote or fast-growing settlements finally get power in their homes, boosting local business and improving quality of life.
key_changes: Roll out the Rural Electricity Acceleration and Urban Intensification Initiative to connect every unserved and under-served community across the country using a Turnkey Implementation Model.
Launch an Electricity Intensification Programme to expand network connections in communities with limited electricity access.
Extend service lines, transformers, and distribution poles to unserved and under-served homes and enterprises.

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: National Policy on Integrated Oil Palm Development
topics.plain_summary: The government is introducing a policy to transform the oil palm sector through increased local cultivation, processing, and a multi-million-dollar finance window designed to help smallholder farmers.
topics.why_it_matters: This policy aims to boost local agricultural production, create hundreds of thousands of jobs, and reduce costly food imports. Farmers benefit directly through financial backing, better seedlings, and guaranteed markets for their harvest.
key_changes: Cultivate 100,000 hectares of new oil palm plantations.
Create over 250,000 direct and indirect jobs across the value chain.
Establish a Dedicated US$500 million Oil Palm Development Finance Window providing long-tenor loans and a five-year moratorium.
Link smallholder farmers directly to nucleus estates and processing facilities through an Outgrower Partnership Scheme.

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: The Big Push Infrastructure Programme and Road Projects
topics.plain_summary: The government is funding major physical infrastructure projects, including an extensive road network programme and a new expressway, to connect the country and ease the transport of agricultural produce and people.
topics.why_it_matters: Bad roads often lead to high food prices and difficult travel. Building and fixing these roads and expressways makes it much easier and cheaper for farmers to get their food to markets safely while reducing travel times for commuters.
key_changes: Add the Accra-Kumasi Expressway and the Ekye Amanfrom-Adawso Bridge to the Big Push Infrastructure Programme.
Implement a three-year programme to construct 1,000 kilometers of agricultural enclave roads implemented by the Department of Feeder Roads.

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: Ghana Secondary Learning Improvement Programme (GSLIP) and Basic Education Support
topics.plain_summary: The government is launching a two-year initiative to eliminate the double-track system in secondary schools, upgrade school facilities, and heavily invest in basic education infrastructure and free textbooks.
topics.why_it_matters: Eliminating the double-track system and improving school buildings means children can return to a normal full-time learning schedule in safer, better-equipped classrooms. Supplying free textbooks and desks also lifts a significant financial burden off parents.
key_changes: Roll out the Ghana Secondary Learning Improvement Programme (GSLIP) to end the double-track system.
Upgrade Category B and Category C schools and complete 30 abandoned E-Blocks.
Construct 200 new Junior High Schools, 200 primary schools, 200 kindergartens, 400 teachers' bungalows, and 400 places of convenience.
Provide free comprehensive curricula-based textbooks and millions of metal desks and chairs.

source_references.section: SECTION 6: FISCAL POLICY MEASURES, STRUCTURAL REFORMS, AND KEY POLICY INITIATIVES

topics.title: 2026 Resource Allocations for Economic Growth and Public Services
topics.plain_summary: The government is rolling out major funding across various sectors for 2026, targeting agriculture, infrastructure, education, health, social protection, and local governance. These investments aim to boost productivity, improve living conditions, create jobs, and support vulnerable groups.
topics.why_it_matters: These resource allocations directly target the daily lives of citizens by injecting funds into critical infrastructure, healthcare, education, and job creation initiatives. Farmers benefit from reduced food inflation and food waste measures, students and parents receive relief through free education policies and school feeding programmes, and patients gain improved access to healthcare and treatment for chronic diseases. Overall, the investments seek to accelerate economic growth and support vulnerable households across the country.

GH¢245 million provided to the Ministry of Food and Agriculture.
GH¢6.9 billion Oil Palm finance window established to support the National Policy on Integrated Oil Palm Development.

topics.title: Economic Recovery and Reform Achievements
topics.plain_summary: The government highlights key economic improvements achieved in under a year, including GDP growth rising to 6.3 percent in early 2025, inflation dropping to 8 percent by October 2025, a stronger cedi, and international reserves climbing to $11.4 billion. Public debt decreased to 45 percent of GDP, and treasury bill rates fell to around 10 percent, easing borrowing pressures.
topics.why_it_matters: These economic shifts aim to stabilize the cost of living for households, lower borrowing costs for the private sector, and restore lost savings and investor confidence following a period of high inflation and currency depreciation.
key_changes: GDP growth rose from 5.3 percent in 2024 to 6.3 percent in the first half of 2025
Inflation dropped sharply from 23.8 percent at the end of December 2024 to single digits, 8 percent, by October 2025
Ghana’s total public debt declined sharply from GH¢726.7 billion (61.8% of GDP) in December 2024 to GH¢630.2 billion (45.0% of GDP) by October 2025

topics.title: Fiscal Governance and Public Financial Management
topics.plain_summary: New legal measures and oversight bodies have been introduced to lock in fiscal discipline. The Public Financial Management Act was amended to cap public debt at 45 percent of GDP by 2034 and mandate a minimum primary surplus. Additionally, an Independent Fiscal Council is set to be constituted in January 2026 to enforce accountability.
topics.why_it_matters: Establishing legal caps on public debt and creating an Independent Fiscal Council aims to prevent reckless government spending, protect public funds from corruption, and ensure long-term economic stability for citizens.
key_changes: The Public Financial Management Act was amended to cap public debt at 45 percent of GDP by 2034 and mandate a minimum primary surplus of 1.5 percent annually
An Independent Fiscal Council has been passed and will be constituted in January 2026 to enforce discipline, transparency, and accountability in public finance

topics.title: Social Protection and Development Programmes
topics.plain_summary: The government has expanded social protection programmes, including LEAP, Free SHS, the NHIS, and targeted food and energy subsidies. Furthermore, development initiatives like the Big Push infrastructure programme and the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme are underway to drive industrial growth and job creation.
topics.why_it_matters: The expansion of social safety nets and infrastructure initiatives directly supports vulnerable households facing hardships while creating new employment opportunities and boosting local industries across the country.
key_changes: The Government expanded LEAP coverage, sustained Free SHS and NHIS, and introduced targeted subsidies for food and energy to cushion the vulnerable
The 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme (24H+) entered full implementation, unlocking industrial growth with a potential to create over 1.7 million jobs by 2028
